extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and instructors (readers of a real-analysis/advanced calculus textbook)
extracted.subtask_short: math textbook appendix: sets and functions
extracted.subtask_description: Appendix-style background covering set theory, functions, basic real-analysis theorems (Mean Value Theorem, inverse function theorem), complex numbers, linear algebra preliminaries, and elementary polynomial facts. Intended to provide definitions, axioms, and standard propositions used elsewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of set-theoretic paradoxes / use of a formal axiom system
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians avoid paradoxes (e.g., Russell paradox) by working within a formal axiom system for sets (e.g., Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory) or by working "informally but carefully" so that sets do not become too "large"; in practice one limits sets to those obtained from other sets by set-theoretic operations and by passage to subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that sets, elements, and membership are taken as primitive and governed by axioms; working informally but carefully is acceptable in practice, but one must take care to avoid treating overly-large collections as sets. Mentions that some authors use "class" for more general collections and suggests avoiding non-set classes when possible; references to further reading (Halmos, Hayden–Kennison, Kelley). Notes there is no proof that this technique avoids problems completely (consistency issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive logical framework and notation for set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory uses primitive terms 'set', 'element', and membership relation ∈; logical connectives ('and', 'or', 'not', 'if...then') and quantifiers ('there exists', 'for all') determine the forms of statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that statements like 'a ∈ S' are meaningful iff a is an element and S is a set. Advises a balance between full formal rigor and practical informality for developing mathematics; indicates some areas (e.g., homological algebra) where certain distinctions must be kept precise (e.g., range vs image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic set operations and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines union (A ∪ B), intersection (A ∩ B), set difference (A \ B), complement (Bc), empty set ∅, power set 2^A, subset/inclusion (A ⊆ B), proper subset (A ⊂ B or A $ B depending on notation), singleton {a}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes notation varies by author (e.g., A \ B vs A − B for difference) and clarifies conventions used in the text. Warns about inconsistent notations in sequences/unordered pairs but states the book will follow traditional conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of unordered pair, ordered pair, Cartesian product, relation, and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Unordered pair {A,B} defined formally; ordered pair (A,B) given formal set-theoretic definition; Cartesian product A × B is set of ordered pairs. A relation between A and B is a subset of A × B. A function f from A to B is a relation with the property that for each x∈A there is exactly one y∈B with (x,y)∈f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides careful distinction: function viewed as a set of ordered pairs together with the domain and range notionally—this careful view makes domain, range, and image meaningful. Mentions alternative informal notations (f(x), f: A → B, x ↦ y) and the use of dot notation f(·) for partial application or holding variables fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, range, codomain, image, and common informal pitfalls about functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain is A, range is a subset of codomain B (some call B the codomain), image f(A) is the subset of B consisting of f(x) for x∈A. With a less careful definition of function (as a rule producing outputs), notions like range may be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that informal habits (calling f(x) the function, conflating range and image) can lead to confusion in algebra and advanced topics; recommends using the more rigorous notation to avoid problems. Gives examples where two functions from A to B might differ despite having same pointwise values if codomains differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice (statement and usage guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiom of Choice: The Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty (equivalently, one can choose one element from each set in an indexed family of nonempty sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that for finite index sets the statement is a theorem, but for infinite (especially uncountable) index sets the axiom is invoked. Gives examples of innocent uses (choosing subsequences in proofs) and notes resulting consequences such as Zorn's Lemma, which is used in later sections; advises that sometimes proofs can be rewritten to avoid invoking the axiom when specific constructive choices are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition, one-to-one, onto, inverse, and restriction of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition: if f:A→B and g:B→C then g◦f: A→C given by g(f(x)). One-to-one (injective): f(x1)=f(x2) ⇒ x1=x2. Onto (surjective onto B): image equals B. If f is one-to-one and onto B, it has a unique inverse f^{-1}: B→A. Restriction f|E denotes function restricted to subset E⊆A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out differences in terminology depending on whether one uses careful or less careful function definitions; recommends stating codomain when claiming 'onto B' to avoid tautology. Explains composition more generally when range of f is subset of domain of g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct and inverse images under functions: algebraic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct image f(E) = {y∈B: y=f(x) for some x∈E} respects unions but not necessarily intersections (f(∪Es)=∪f(Es), but f(∩Es) ⊆ ∩f(Es) may be proper). Inverse image f^{-1}(T) = {x∈A: f(x)∈T} respects unions, intersections, and complements with standard identities (f^{-1}(∪Es)=∪f^{-1}(Es), f^{-1}(∩Es)=∩f^{-1}(Es), f^{-1}(Tc)=(f^{-1}(T))c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit examples showing equality can fail for direct images under intersections; emphasizes that inverse images behave well with set-theoretic operations. Provides proofs/sketches of the identities for inverse images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean Value Theorem and Rolle-type lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma (Rolle-like): If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b) then there exists c∈(a,b) with f'(c)=0. Mean Value Theorem: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) then f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) for some c in (a,b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes proof sketches (use of maximum/minimum and application of the lemma to a constructed function). Presents two standard corollaries: (1) If f'≡0 on (a,b) then f is constant; (2) If f'>0 everywhere then f is strictly increasing. Also discusses endpoint differentiability extension when derivative has finite limit approaching endpoint and continuity of the extended derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension notion: continuous derivative at endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: If f' has a finite limit as x approaches an endpoint (from inside the interval), one can extend f to include the endpoint so that the extended function is differentiable at the endpoint and its derivative is continuous there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives construction for extension F(x)=f(x)−f(a)−C(x−a) for left endpoint with C = lim_{x→a+} f'(x) and shows F'(a)=C; explains meaning of phrase 'has a continuous derivative at an endpoint'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse Function Theorem in one variable (statement and derivative formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:(a,b)→R has a continuous everywhere-positive derivative, then f is strictly increasing, its image is an interval (c,d), the inverse g:(c,d)→(a,b) exists, and g'(y)=1 / f'(g(y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: uses Mean Value Theorem and bounds on f' to show g is differentiable and deduces the derivative formula; also notes continuity of g' follows from continuity of f' and composition. Emphasizes condition that f' be nowhere zero (positive here) to ensure monotonicity and invertibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers: algebraic structure, conjugation, absolute value, triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex numbers C are a two-dimensional real vector space with basis {1,i} where i^2=−1. Conjugation z↦z̄, real and imaginary parts Re z = (z+z̄)/2, Im z = (z−z̄)/(2i). Absolute value |z| satisfies |z|^2 = z z̄, multiplicativity |zw| = |z||w|, and the triangle inequality |z+w| ≤ |z|+|w|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives algebraic properties and quick verification sketches (e.g., expanding (z+w)(z̄+w̄) and using Re(z w̄)≤|z||w| to derive triangle inequality). Notes the common practice of writing a+bi with a,b∈R and provides simple examples/formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz (Cauchy–Schwarz) inequality for complex n-tuples
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex n-tuples (a1,...,an) and (b1,...,bn), the Schwarz inequality states (∑|ak bk|)^2 ≤ (∑|ak|^2)(∑|bk|^2) (classically written as |∑ ak b̄k|^2 ≤ (∑|ak|^2)(∑|bk|^2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a short proof idea: consider quadratic form ∥a−λb∥^2 ≥ 0 and choose λ appropriately; remarks that in classical setting often called Cauchy–Schwarz and that generalizations drop personal names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relations and quotient by equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation '∼' on set S is a subset of S×S satisfying reflexivity (a∼a), symmetry (a∼b ⇒ b∼a), and transitivity (a∼b and b∼c ⇒ a∼c). The equivalence class [a] = {b∈S: a∼b} and equivalence classes partition S: any two classes are equal or disjoint, and S is union of classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives elementary example on Z (a∼b if a−b is even), and discusses application to constructions in the text (e.g., passing from pseudometrics to metrics or considering homeomorphism classes). Notes caution about defining equivalence on classes that are not sets and a workaround (restrict to a subclass that is a set).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between linear transformations and matrices; rank-nullity
rubrics_metrics.description: Linear transformations T: F^n→F^m correspond uniquely to m-by-n matrices A via T(x)=Ax with columns given by T(e_j). Kernel of T corresponds to null space of A; image corresponds to column space. The dimension identities yield dim(domain)=dim(kernel)+dim(image) and rank equals dimension of column (or row) span.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies conventions (column-vector convention, standard bases e_j and u_i). Notes that composition of linear maps corresponds to matrix multiplication in the same written order. Gives examples (e.g., rotation matrix in R^2) and explains notation A_{ij} for matrix entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant: defining properties and consequences (i)–(ix)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinant det: square matrices → F is uniquely defined by: (i) linearity in each row holding others fixed; (ii) det 0 if two rows are equal; (iii) det I = 1. Consequences listed: (iv) det A = 0 iff A noninvertible; (v) det A^T = det A; (vi) det(cA)=c^n det A for scalar c, n×n matrix; (vii) det(AB)=det A · det B; (viii) permutation formula and cofactor expansion; (ix) Cramer's rule: solution x of Ax=b has x_j = det A_j / det A when det A ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how row operations affect determinant (row addition leaves det unchanged, row swap multiplies det by −1, scaling a row scales det) and how these lead to calculation by row reduction. States cofactor expansion formula and gives application to solving linear systems (Cramer's rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomials: representation, degree, evaluation, and roots (beginning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynomials with coefficients in field F (R or C) are sequences (a0,a1,...,an,0,0,...) with finitely many nonzero terms, denoted P(X)=a0 + a1 X + ... + an X^n. The degree deg P is highest n with an ≠ 0. If r∈F then P(r) denotes evaluation; r is a root if P(r)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the convenience of treating polynomials as sequences of coefficients and the usual algebraic operations (addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication) making the polynomial ring with standard properties. (Section continues beyond this chunk toward unique factorization and roots.)
